analysis.one_liner: Gives federal tax credits, up to $5 billion a year, for donations to private-school scholarship funds.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House; it sat in two committees until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let individuals and corporations claim a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit for cash donated to nonprofit scholarship organizations that pay for elementary and secondary education, including private and religious schools. Total credits would be capped at $5 billion per year, with the money allocated among states and weighted toward children from low-income families. Donors would get their tax money back in the form of a credit while deciding how it is spent, and the bill would bar any federal control over private, religious, or home-school providers receiving the funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who want to use scholarships for private or religious schooling would gain a new, federally subsidized funding stream. Donors with federal income tax liability — individuals up to 10% of their income and corporations up to 5% of taxable income — could redirect taxes they would otherwise owe into scholarship funds. Private schools and the scholarship organizations themselves would gain a large new revenue channel.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private schools, donors, and scholarship organizations

how_it_helps.text: Individuals could claim a tax credit equal to their full cash contribution to an eligible scholarship-granting organization, up to 10% of adjusted gross income, with unused credit carried forward for up to five years [S3].
Domestic corporations could claim the same credit up to 5% of taxable income, with the credit counting toward the general business credit [S3].

Scholarships could be used for a student's elementary or secondary education as recognized by the state, including career and technical education, and the bill forbids states from disadvantaging religious or home-school providers [S3].

In allocating the $5 billion national cap among states, 80% of the remaining pool each year would be weighted toward children from families below the poverty line, and no state would receive less than one-half of one percent of the annual allotment [S3].
Scholarship amounts would not count as income of the child or parents for federal tax purposes or for determining eligibility for other federal programs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would forgo up to $5 billion per year in revenue that donors otherwise owed. Public schools would face a slower erosion: as students leave with scholarships funded by redirected tax dollars, the tax base that supports public education for everyone else shrinks. Taxpayers who do not use the program would bear the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury and public school funding

drawbacks.text: The credit is nonrefundable — it cannot exceed the donor's federal income tax liability for the year [S3] — so the direct tax benefit flows only to people and corporations that owe income tax, while families with little or no tax liability get no donor-side benefit.
The program would cost the Treasury up to $5 billion a year in forgone revenue [S2], money that could otherwise fund public services including public schools.

The bill expressly prohibits any federal control over private, religious, or home education providers receiving scholarship-funded students [S3], leaving the receiving schools outside public accountability standards that apply to public schools.
Because donations are directed by donors rather than elected bodies, public money would be steered to education providers through a channel no legislature appropriates or oversees directly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give some families real help affording private school and would weight new money toward low-income children. But it does this by letting donors decide where up to $5 billion a year of tax revenue goes, with the tax benefit concentrated among households and corporations that owe income tax, and with no federal accountability over the private providers receiving the money. Weighing the design honestly: a direct appropriation or refundable scholarship program could deliver the same help to low-income students at lower cost and with public oversight; this design instead builds a permanent, donor-directed funding channel for private education.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees, neither of which ever considered it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bradley Byrne introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, the Committee on Education and Labor [S1] [S5].
110 House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats appear among its cosponsors [S4].
The full action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the initial referral [S5].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and public school funding were spared the $5 billion-a-year revenue diversion, and the scholarship organizations and private schools that would have gained a new subsidized revenue stream gained nothing. Families hoping for federally funded private-school scholarships were the losers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury and public school funding

sides.party_line_note: All 110 cosponsors were Republicans — 110 of the 197 House Republicans — and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; Democratic committee chairs declined to act on it.

industries.industry: Private K-12 schools, including religious schools
industries.note: The bill would create a federal tax-credit pipeline paying private and religious school tuition through scholarship organizations, with an explicit prohibition on federal control over those providers. The revenue comes from taxes otherwise owed to the Treasury, which funds public education for everyone else.

The bill would make these 501(c)(3) intermediaries the permanent required channel for up to $5 billion a year in tax-credited education money, with at least 90% of contributions required to flow to scholarships. Donors, not any public body, would decide which organizations receive the money.

Because the credit cannot exceed tax liability, the direct benefit goes only to households and corporations that owe federal income tax, letting them redirect taxes they would otherwise pay. Families without income tax liability get no donor-side benefit.

Every dollar claimed as a credit is federal revenue not collected, shrinking the base available for public services, and students leaving with scholarships reduce enrollment-based funding. Public schools serve all children regardless of where they live or whether any provider will take them.
